demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: keep mind occupied all the time

Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't trust that I will do the right thing
My life has been destroyed by the trauma
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within Memory, 'Feels Present Not Past' and 'Full Sensory Reliving' indicate highly intrusive, poorly contextualized trauma memory, which conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' These can sometimes coexist, but stated this strongly they pull in opposite directions and are hard to reconcile as the same memory profile.

issues.item: Threat: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: The Threat items depict pervasive fear of being physically attacked by other people ('watch other people closely', 'back to wall', 'stay alert at night'), which does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another. For this trauma, threat is more plausibly guilt, condemnation, or fear of consequences, not generalized interpersonal danger.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Mirror Checking' is not well linked to the rest of the profile. Nothing in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Negative Appraisals suggests appearance-focused concern, dissociation needing visual reassurance, or checking for injury; as selected, it appears clinically disconnected.

Mirror checking is hard to reconcile with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; it more strongly suggests concerns about visible injury, appearance, or being followed, none of which are supported by the other nodes.

issues.item: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: Back-to-wall hypervigilance and scanning the room imply an interpersonal or attack-related threat context. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which centers on guilt, reliving, and self-blame after accidentally injuring someone rather than danger from other people.

vignette: Tyler had always taken pride in his work as a school counselor, but that sense of purpose was shattered on a fateful day two years ago. He was driving home from a particularly grueling parent-teacher conference when he failed to stop at an intersection, striking another vehicle and seriously injuring its occupant. The memory of the crash, and the weight of responsibility for someone else's pain, has haunted him ever since. As Tyler recounts that day, his eyes glaze over, and his voice takes on a detached quality, as if observing himself from outside his body. "I keep thinking about what I could've done differently," he says, his mind replaying the scene like a looped recording. The smell of smoke and gasoline still transports him back to that moment, making his heart racing with anxiety. The aftermath of the accident was a blur of police reports, medical procedures, and anxious visits to the hospital to check on the injured party's progress. Tyler became intensely focused on avoiding anything that might remind him of that day – from steering clear of intersections that looked similar to the one where he crashed to refusing to think about what had happened. He even started taking a longer route home from work to avoid driving past the scene. At school, Tyler found it increasingly difficult to connect with his students and colleagues. The constant mental distraction required to suppress memories of the accident left him exhausted and on edge. Even during meetings or conversations, his mind would start to wander back to that day, making it hard for him to focus. His relationships began to suffer – his wife grew concerned about his distant behavior, while his colleagues started noticing a decline in his usually empathetic approach. As time went by, Tyler became convinced that the accident had destroyed his life, eroding his confidence as a counselor and a person. He struggled to fall asleep at night, lying awake with his ears tuned for any sign of sirens or other noise that might signal another disaster. When memories of the crash did surface, they came back in vivid detail – the crunching sound, the feeling of weightlessness, the overwhelming sense of dread. The sensations were so real it felt as if he was reliving them all over again. During sessions with his therapist, Tyler's struggle to put words to what happened becomes apparent. He falters when trying to describe the event, often trailing off or changing subjects abruptly. When probed gently about this difficulty, he reveals a crippling sense of self-doubt: "I just can't trust that I'll do the right thing anymore," he confesses, his voice barely above a whisper. Tyler's growing anxiety and avoidance behaviors have taken a toll on his relationship with his wife, Rachel. She has tried to be supportive, but her frustration is starting to show – she feels like she's lost the man she married, and doesn't know how to reach him anymore. As their anniversary approaches, Tyler finds himself dreading it – another painful reminder of what he sees as a failed life. It was this fear of losing Rachel, combined with his inability to shake off the memories of the accident, that finally pushed Tyler to seek help. He's now sitting in therapy, trying to unravel the complex web of emotions and self-blame that has taken hold of him. What terrifies him most is the thought of never being able to regain control over his life – or himself.
